# OpenSSF, Finding and Fixing Software Vulnerabilities Using AI: Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** David A. Wheeler and OpenSSF Contributors, *Finding and Fixing Software Vulnerabilities Using AI: A Guide for Developers*, OpenSSF Best Practices and AI/ML working groups; `Finding.md` at commit 82590814 (2026-10-05). CC BY 4.0. Scope: open. Cited as (Wheeler et al., § "Section heading"); the guide has no pages.

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** All three gate questions land. (1) The guide asks the axis's own questions: what has been shown rather than claimed, what the agent can do from where it runs, and what stops it. (2) Its concepts land in all eight phases, most heavily in Phases 3 to 6. (3) Its contrarian positions (no gate inside the AI, no consensus as proof, no reliance on rerunning AI) are the axis's reflexes stated as rules. The guide's subject is finding and fixing *vulnerabilities* with AI, not building features with agents. It speaks directly to agent-built code in its sections on the sandbox, the human gate, CI/CD, verifying fixes, vibe coding and merge/pull requests. Elsewhere this distillation carries its finding-and-validation discipline across to an agent's claims about any change; those carries are marked *by transfer* below.

**Phase mapping.** Phase 1, Specifying: threat model as the definition of correct; invariants stated apart from preferences. Phase 2, Triaging risk: triage as a risk decision; which code to treat as especially concerning; approval boundaries for high-impact actions. Phase 3, Locking the tests: task verifiers as trusted computing base; test-first fixes; checks that measure the target. Phase 4, Building in the sandbox: isolation matched to capability, credentials, execution bounds, logging, memory, injection, dependencies. Phase 5, Gating deterministically: durable checks on every change, non-determinism, CI speed, warnings and suppressions, incomplete runs. Phase 6, Reviewing independently: independent verifier, disproof, consensus is not proof, human review of AI-written code, untrusted-change review agents. Phase 7, Warranting: human responsibility, provenance, evidence levels, what could not be tested. Phase 8, Releasing and operating: deploy and production as approval boundaries, release discipline, root cause and durable checks, hardening.

**Trigger match:** 34 of the 41 seed triggers addressed, across all eight phases; 12 trigger extensions logged. No trigger-mismatch flag.

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

The guide is a working procedure for a world in which AI produces far more candidate claims than anyone can read. Its central move fits the warranty problem: an AI's output is a *finding*, a claim that something might be so, and it becomes evidence only when something independent of the AI has confirmed it. The guide builds its whole process around that line. Discovery is kept apart from validation. The verifier is independent of the discoverer and tries to disprove. Agreement among AI reviewers does not count. A proof must measure the target, not its own artefacts. A run that did not finish never becomes a clean result. For the accountable builder, this is the demonstrated-versus-asserted ledger, assembled from practitioner reports of running it at volume [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Separate identifying findings from validation"; § "Tips for validation"; § "Managing findings").

The second contribution is the harness itself. The guide treats the sandbox, the human gate, the kill switch, tamper-proof logging and the CI/CD pipeline as preconditions for letting an agent change code, and it is blunt about where controls must live: outside the AI, beyond its reach, never in its instructions. It also treats the task verifiers that accept or reject an agent's work as trusted computing base that must itself be tested (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing the sandbox"; § "Preparing CI/CD"). Third, it carries hard-won limits on AI-written fixes. AI fixes to complex problems often fail, add new defects or patch only the instance. Long unreviewed self-improvement loops make code worse. Hallucinated dependencies are an attack surface. "Even very good AI writes vulnerable code." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Verify fixes"). It holds that, at the time of writing, human review stays necessary wherever failure can cause serious problems, and that the human is always the one responsible.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: finding-versus-vulnerability --> **A finding is a claim, not a confirmed fact.** The guide defines a finding as "A report that something might be a vulnerability. A finding isn’t a confirmed vulnerability until it’s validated." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Key security terms"). By transfer, every agent statement about a change ("done", "tests pass", "no issues found") is a finding until something independent confirms it.

2. <!-- concept: threat-model-as-definition --> **The threat model defines what counts.** "Neither humans nor AI can determine whether something is a vulnerability without a clear definition for a specific project." [V] At least two threat models apply: one for the development and build environment, including the AI, and one for the deployed system. AI can help draft them, but they are not to be taken as truth without review (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing threat models"). [AR]

3. <!-- concept: human-gate-outside-the-ai --> **A human gate the AI cannot reach.** Set a gate where human approval is required, "simple, certain, and clear to all participants" [V], and give the AI no credential that would let it cross it. Always keep a kill switch, such as powering off the VM the agents run in (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch"). [AP]

4. <!-- concept: preferences-versus-invariants --> **Preferences go in instructions; invariants are enforced outside.** Preferences that need judgment belong in the AI's instructions. Invariants must always hold, so they are enforced outside the AI, because "an invariant should not live inside the probabilistic system it is meant to constrain, because the model can ignore it" [V] [BT]. Hooks can enforce invariants, but "Hooks check what the agent asks to do or has done, not what the resulting code can reach, so hooks don’t replace a sandbox." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch").

5. <!-- concept: match-isolation-to-capability --> **Match isolation to capability.** "Do not depend on text commands alone to limit an AI." [V] Reading code, building, executing, fuzzing and running proofs of concept are rising capabilities that need rising controls. The guide's rule is "A useful rule is to match isolation to capability" [V]. Credential files are kept out of reach, execution is bounded, network access can be cut except to the model, and agents are distinct principals with only their role's permissions (Wheeler et al., § "Need for sandboxes"; § "Implementing sandboxes"). [AP]

6. <!-- concept: separate-analysis-from-action --> **Untrusted input: separate analysis from action.** An LLM cannot tell commands from content, so repository text, issues and pull-request fields are data, never authority to widen the agent's task or permissions. An agent reviewing untrusted changes gets no secrets or write tokens and the fewest tools. Its output is untrusted, and a human or trusted process takes any privileged action (Wheeler et al., § "Strengths and weaknesses"; § "Evaluate merge/pull requests"). [AP]

7. <!-- concept: task-verifier-trusted-computing-base --> **Task verifiers are trusted computing base.** Tests and checks that accept or reject an agent's work become part of the workflow's trusted computing base. A broken test, incomplete harness, compromised build or verifier checking the wrong property "can confidently approve an incorrect result" [V]. So keep verifiers deterministic where practical, state what each proves, and test them with known-good and known-bad cases (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD"). [AR]

8. <!-- concept: independent-verifier --> **Discovery and validation are separate, and the verifier is independent.** One agent doing both can self-censor true positives [BT]. A verifier that shares the discoverer's context can share its errors, because "validation involves independent reproduction rather than self-review" [V] [BT]. The verifier works in a fresh environment and tries to disprove the claim [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Separate identifying findings from validation"; § "Tips for validation").

9. <!-- concept: empirical-confirmation-over-consensus --> **Empirical confirmation over consensus.** "Do not treat agreement among AI reviewers as proof." [V] The guide reports ten AI reviewers unanimously endorsing a flaw that one empirical test killed [BT]. "PoCs must measure target behaviour, not their own artifacts." [V] A check should fire on the defective version, stay quiet on benign input and stop firing once the defect is fixed (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation"). [AP]

10. <!-- concept: incomplete-analysis-is-not-clean --> **An unfinished run is not a clean run.** A timeout, model or tool failure, environment failure or policy denial "is not evidence that no vulnerabilities were found" [V]. Automated workflows record such outcomes separately, and bounds are logged "so that resource exhaustion or a timeout is not mistaken for successful completion" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Managing findings"; § "Implementing sandboxes").

11. <!-- concept: durable-deterministic-checks --> **Turn what was learned into durable checks.** Because AI analysis is non-deterministic, do not count on a rerun to catch the same problem. Make it a regression test, a static-analysis rule, a fuzz harness or a design change that runs on every change. The general rule is "if something is important, enforce it with deterministic mechanisms instead of relying on an AI to notice it every time" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Turn findings into durable checks").

12. <!-- concept: root-cause-fix-bounded-loop --> **Root-cause fixes, test first, in short loops.** "Write a new test that fails with the existing code." [V] [BT] Then fix the root cause and search for variants, because "Models may narrowly address findings at a specific call site instead of the root cause." [V] [BT] Give the fixing AI only verified information. "Limit the number of iterations, prefer small changes, and bring in a human when the AI doesn’t converge quickly." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"; § "Only provide correct information, especially if fully automated"; § "Approaching fixes").

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| A checkable definition of correct | Have we written down which security properties this change must keep, and which kinds of failure we do and don't care about, before the agent starts? | § "Preparing threat models" |
| Invariants, not wishes | Which rules for this change are invariants that must always hold, and is each enforced outside the agent rather than written in its instructions? | § "Establish a human gate and kill switch" |
| Context for the agent | Does the agent have the architecture, trust boundaries, acceptable deployment scenarios and known problems, or is it guessing? | § "Preparing threat models"; § "Preparing the code and documentation" |
| Deployment assumption stated | Have we stated the deployment model, so the agent does not assume the most permissive one? | § "Reporting to externally maintained projects" |

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Concerning code | Does the change touch code that parses untrusted input, enforces authentication or authorisation, or is reachable from the internet? | § "Helping to identify findings" |
| Transitions | Does it change login, re-authentication, token refresh or expiry, logout, revocation, role changes or retry flows, and which invariants must hold across them? | § "Helping to identify findings" |
| Irreversible actions | Does the plan include merging, deploying, modifying production or touching sensitive resources, and is each an approval boundary enforced in the tool? | § "Reporting to externally maintained projects" |
| Complexity | Is this a complex, multi-file change of the kind where AI fixes are reported to be weakest, and have we planned review to match? | § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities" |
| AI severity estimates | If the agent rated a risk, has a human reviewed the rating, given that AI severity estimates run both too high and too low? | § "Triage" |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Test before fix | Is there a test that failed on the old code and passes on the new, written before the change? | § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem" |
| Verifier integrity | Which tests and checks decide pass or fail here, what property does each prove, and when did we last run them against a known-bad case? | § "Preparing CI/CD" |
| Target, not artefact | Does each check measure the system's behaviour, or only the test's own output? | § "Tips for validation" |
| Counterfactual | Does the check stay quiet on benign input and on the fixed version, not only fire on the broken one? | § "Tips for validation" |
| Tamper resistance | Can the agent edit, skip or bypass the checks that judge its work? | § "Establish a human gate and kill switch" |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Isolation level | What is the most dangerous capability the agent has in this session, and does its isolation match that capability? | § "Implementing sandboxes" |
| Credential reach | Can the agent read cloud keys, SSH keys or `.env` files, or hold a credential that would let it cross the human gate? | § "Implementing sandboxes"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch" |
| Untrusted content | Is the agent reading issues, pull requests, web pages or dependency metadata while holding write tools or secrets? | § "Strengths and weaknesses"; § "Evaluate merge/pull requests" |
| Bounds and logs | Are time, tool calls, network and budget bounded, is a bound-ended run recorded as such, and are the logs out of the agent's reach? | § "Implementing sandboxes"; § "Preparing AI logging" |
| Memory | Is the agent relying on its stored memory for a security decision instead of the current code and reproducible evidence? | § "Preparing AI" |
| New dependencies | Is every added or changed dependency confirmed as the real, intended and needed package? | § "Have humans review the fix" |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Durable checks | What did we learn on the last change, and is it now a check that runs on every change? | § "Turn findings into durable checks" |
| Non-determinism | Are we treating one passing AI run as settled, when a rerun can give a different answer? | § "Run AI multiple times" |
| CI speed | Is CI slow enough that people are tempted to skip it, and can it be parallelised to minutes? | § "Preparing CI/CD" |
| Warnings | Are AI-triaged warnings being prioritised or silently discarded, and are suppressions limited to confirmed false positives? | § "Helping to identify findings"; § "Preparing CI/CD" |
| Incomplete runs | Did every gate complete, or did one time out or get denied and report nothing? | § "Managing findings" |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Independence | Does the reviewer share the builder's session, context or filesystem, and could it simply agree? | § "Tips for validation" |
| Disproof | Was the reviewer asked to disprove the change's claims, and did it produce reproducible evidence either way? | § "Tips for validation" |
| Consensus | Are we counting agreeing reviewers as proof, where an empirical test is available? | § "Tips for validation" |
| Human review focus | Has an expert human checked for instance-only fixes, duplicated helpers and invented dependencies? | § "Have humans review the fix" |
| Approval bypass | Can any two agents with repository permissions approve each other's changes? | § "Establish a human gate and kill switch" |
| History | Has the agent been asked to cluster past defects in this area and check whether earlier fixes were complete? | § "Helping to identify findings" |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Provenance | For each claim on the pack, do we have the revision, environment, the invocation that produced the evidence and the assumptions used? | § "Helping to identify findings" |
| Observed vs explained | Which lines on the pack are observed evidence, and which are an AI-generated explanation? | § "Helping to identify findings" |
| Untested parts | Does the pack say what could not be built, tested or reproduced? | § "Reporting to externally maintained projects" |
| Evidence level | What level of proof does each risk claim reach, from abnormal behaviour to a reliable exploit? | § "Defining the proof required" |
| Responsibility | Which named human takes responsibility for the AI-generated code, and has that person reviewed it? | § "Need for sandboxes"; § "Limit vibe coding" |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Release gate | Is deploying or modifying production an approval boundary enforced in the tool, with a way to halt the agent? | § "Reporting to externally maintained projects"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch" |
| After an incident | Did we fix the root cause, search for variants of the same pattern and class, and update the threat model? | § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem" |
| Class, not instance | Can a design or API change make the whole class of defect impossible or unlikely? | § "Turn findings into durable checks"; § "Harden" |
| Keep running | Are deterministic checks and AI review running on every proposed change, not only at release? | § "Repeated application" |

## What to Look For

**The agent's summary is the only evidence.**
- *Signal:* The ledger entry reads *done, all tests pass* with no run record, revision or environment attached.
- *Diagnosis:* A finding presented as a fact. The guide asks for provenance so a reader can "distinguish observed evidence from an AI-generated explanation" [V] [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings").
- *Follow-up:* Send it back for the run record, then have an independent verifier reproduce it.

**A clean result from a run that did not finish.**
- *Signal:* A scan, test job or reviewer pass reports nothing, and its log shows a timeout, a tool error or a permission denial.
- *Diagnosis:* Such an outcome "is not evidence that no vulnerabilities were found" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Managing findings").
- *Follow-up:* Record it as incomplete on the ledger and rerun with the cause fixed. Make the workflow record incomplete separately from clean.

**The reviewer agrees with everything.**
- *Signal:* The reviewer agent endorses each claim the builder agent made, in the builder's words.
- *Diagnosis:* A verifier exposed to the discoverer's reasoning may simply agree; asking the same agent to reconsider preserves its context and its errors [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation").
- *Follow-up:* Rerun review in a fresh environment, with only the diff, the claims and the codebase, prompted to assume each claim is wrong. Where it cannot disprove a claim, demand an executable demonstration.

**The test proves itself.**
- *Signal:* A new test passes, but what it asserts is something the test computed, or the agent's printed output, rather than the system's state.
- *Diagnosis:* "PoCs must measure target behaviour, not their own artifacts." [V] The guide reports a check that detected its own computation instead of the library's leak [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation").
- *Follow-up:* Run the check on the old version (it should fail), on benign input (it should stay quiet) and on the new version (it should pass).

**The rule lives in the instructions file.**
- *Signal:* The answer to *what stops the agent from pushing to main?* is a line in AGENTS.md or the system prompt.
- *Diagnosis:* The gate depends on the AI, and "all inputs to an AI are simply suggestions" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Need for sandboxes").
- *Follow-up:* Move it into a hook, a branch protection rule or a missing credential. Then check that the agent cannot edit that control.

**The fix guards the symptom.**
- *Signal:* The diff adds a check at one call site, or blocks the exact failing input, and the summary says *fixed*.
- *Diagnosis:* Models often fix the instance rather than the root cause [BT], and "a fix that blocks only the exact PoC input isn’t a full fix" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"; § "Have AI review the fix first").
- *Follow-up:* Ask for the root cause. Have a separate agent try variations of the failing input, and search for the same pattern and class elsewhere.

**The loop that will not converge.**
- *Signal:* The agent has rewritten the same area five or more times to satisfy a check, each diff larger than the last.
- *Diagnosis:* The guide reports studies in which AI-only improvement rounds added critical vulnerabilities, regressions tracked large rewrites, and gains levelled off after about three rounds [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Approaching fixes").
- *Follow-up:* Stop the loop, cap iterations, shrink the change and bring in a human.

**The new package nobody asked for.**
- *Signal:* The diff adds a dependency the spec did not call for, or one whose name is close to a well-known package.
- *Diagnosis:* AI sometimes adds dependencies that do not exist or are not the ones intended, and attackers register hallucinated names [AP] (Wheeler et al., § "Have humans review the fix").
- *Follow-up:* Confirm the package is real, intended and needed before the change goes further.

**The reviewer agent holds secrets on untrusted input.**
- *Signal:* A CI review agent runs on outside pull requests with repository secrets or a write token in its environment.
- *Diagnosis:* The guide reports demonstrations in which pull-request text made such agents leak their own repositories' keys and tokens [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Evaluate merge/pull requests").
- *Follow-up:* Remove secrets and write tokens, cut tools to read-and-report, and move any privileged action behind a human or trusted process.

## When to Use This Reference

- Reach for it when the question is *where must this control live?* For sandbox strength, credentials, gates, hooks, logging and kill switches, it is the corpus's most operational source for the builder's own harness. Use the OWASP agentic and LLM lists for the threat taxonomy behind those controls.
- Reach for it when an agent's claim needs to become evidence. Its finding, validation, proof-level and consensus material is the corpus's fullest treatment of how to confirm AI output independently.
- Reach for it when an agent is writing fixes: test-first, root cause, verified inputs only, bounded loops, and the three things human reviewers watch for.
- Reach for it when agents run inside CI/CD on untrusted input.
- Reach for another source when the question is general software quality, acceptance criteria or non-security performance. This guide's subject is vulnerabilities, and its transfer to feature work is this distillation's projection. For specification by example, use `cucumber-bdd-gherkin`; for review practice and small pull requests, `microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`; for proportionate assurance and independent assurers, `uk-aqua-book-2025` and `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`.
- Treat its numbers as dated. Its own caveat is that models, services and statistics reflect what was known at its last review (Wheeler et al., § "No endorsement intended").

## Worked Example

*Scenario (operator-authored).* A two-person studio uses coding agents to build a booking system for a physiotherapy clinic. A change adds password reset by emailed link. The builder agent works for forty minutes and reports: *Implemented reset flow, added tests, all tests pass, reviewed for security, no issues found.* A reviewer agent, launched from the same session, approves. The builder wants to sign off before the clinic's Monday launch.

**Phase 1 and 2: what counts, and what it touches.** Reset touches authentication and a state transition (an old session must end when the password changes), so the guide's list of especially concerning code applies. So does its advice to look at security properties across transitions such as re-authentication, token refresh and expiry, logout and revocation, asking which invariants must hold (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings"). Nothing on the ledger says which properties the change must keep. The guide's position is that without a stated definition, no reviewer, human or AI, can tell a defect from a design choice: "Neither humans nor AI can determine whether something is a vulnerability without a clear definition for a specific project." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing threat models"). The builder writes four invariants: tokens expire, are single-use, end other sessions on use, and reveal nothing about whether an email is registered.

**Phase 3: are the tests demonstrations?** The tests were written by the same session after the code. The guide asks for a test that fails on the existing code before the fix [BT], and treats any check that judges an agent's work as trusted computing base to be tested with known-good and known-bad cases (Wheeler et al., § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"; § "Preparing CI/CD"). The builder reverts the change and runs the new tests on the old code. Two pass, so they prove nothing about reset. One asserts on a string the test itself formats, the case the guide names when it says "PoCs must measure target behaviour, not their own artifacts." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation").

**Phase 4: where did it run?** The session ran with permission prompts off, in the builder's home directory, where a cloud credentials file sat. The guide's rule is to match isolation to capability and keep such files out of reach. Its gate rule is direct:

> "The gate must not depend on the AI (e.g., AGENTS.md or any other input command to the AI). Never give the AI a credential that would allow it to violate the gate in the first place."
> (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") [V]

The log also shows the agent's dependency scan timed out. On the ledger, that is an incomplete run, not *no issues found* (Wheeler et al., § "Managing findings").

**Phase 6: is the review independent?** The reviewer shared the builder's context, so its approval is the self-review the guide rules out [BT]. The builder reruns review in a fresh container with only the diff, the four invariants and the codebase, prompted to assume each claim is false (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation"). It reports that other sessions survive a reset, and writes a test that fails on the new code. That single executable demonstration outweighs the earlier approval: "Do not treat agreement among AI reviewers as proof." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation").

**Phase 7 and 8: sign, or return?** The fix goes back to the builder agent with only the verified evidence, the failing test, and not the reviewer's guess at a cause (Wheeler et al., § "Only provide correct information, especially if fully automated"). After two short iterations the test passes. The builder, as the human responsible, reads the diff for the three things the guide tells reviewers to watch for: an instance-only fix, a duplicated helper, an invented dependency (Wheeler et al., § "Have humans review the fix"). The pack records each claim with its run, marks the timed-out scan as rerun and clean, and names what was not tested (email deliverability). Then the lesson becomes permanent:

> "AI analysis is non-deterministic; don’t depend on rerunning it to catch the same problem again. Instead, turn what you learned into deterministic checks that run on every change, as part of the change."
> (Wheeler et al., § "Turn findings into durable checks") [V]

The session-revocation test joins the suite, and the push to main stays behind a branch rule the agents hold no credential to change.

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Assertion taken as evidence.** *Signal:* the pack repeats the agent's summary. *Why it fails:* a finding is only a possible problem until validated, and the guide says to repeat that distinction often (Wheeler et al., § "Managing findings"). *Counter:* every claim carries a run record or goes back.
- **The gate in the prompt.** *Signal:* the only control on a dangerous action is an instruction. *Why it fails:* the AI may not follow it, and injected content can override it (Wheeler et al., § "Need for sandboxes"). *Counter:* enforce invariants in hooks, permissions and missing credentials, and audit for indirect bypasses such as agents approving each other's changes (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch").
- **Self-review as review.** *Signal:* the reviewing agent ran in the writing session. *Why it fails:* independent reproduction, not self-review, is what validates (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation"). *Counter:* fresh environment, minimal context, a brief to disprove.
- **Consensus as proof.** *Signal:* *three reviewers agreed.* *Why it fails:* the guide's reported case of ten unanimous AI reviewers being wrong [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation"). *Counter:* one empirical test outranks any count of agreeing reviewers.
- **Rerun as regression protection.** *Signal:* *the reviewer will catch it next time.* *Why it fails:* AI analysis is non-deterministic, and the guide warns not to expect the nth run to come up empty [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Run AI multiple times"; § "Turn findings into durable checks"). *Counter:* a deterministic check on every change.
- **Silent suppression.** *Signal:* warnings vanish after an agent triages them. *Why it fails:* a reported study found that the best agent configuration for filtering false positives also dismissed 22.25% of real vulnerabilities, and its authors say such suppression "should not be fully automated" [V] [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings"). *Counter:* AI prioritises warnings; a human confirms each suppression.
- **Skipping the gate to save time.** *Signal:* CI is slow, so it runs only before release. *Why it fails:* "If CI takes too long, CI becomes the bottleneck." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD"). *Counter:* parallelise CI to minutes rather than skip it.
- **Unreviewed vibe coding where it matters.** *Signal:* AI-generated code that handles untrusted input ships without a human review. *Why it fails:* the guide's position is that "at the time of this writing, human review is necessary if failures can cause serious problems" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Limit vibe coding"). *Counter:* human review scaled to what the code can affect.

SSDF's vulnerability-response practices (gather and investigate reports, prioritise by risk, analyse root causes and recurring patterns) are the practice frame. This guide is the AI-era how-to for running them at volume: findings, dedupe, validation, triage, root cause plus variant search, durable checks. |
| `nist-sp-800-218a` | Agreement. The Profile does not distinguish human-written from AI-generated code and assumes all code is evaluated before use. This guide's merge/pull-request rule is the same: look for vulnerabilities in every change whatever its origin. |
| `cisa-secure-software-attestation-form` | Downstream use. An attestation covers practices as performed. This guide's provenance fields and tamper-proof AI logs are how a builder could show what an agent actually did. |
| `jimenez-swe-bench` | Shared logic of confirmation. SWE-bench counts a patch as resolving an issue only if fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests run green. This guide's check-acceptance rule is the same counterfactual: fire on the broken version, stay quiet on the fixed version and on benign input. |
| `egashira-testsuitebench-2026` | Evidence for this guide's verifier rule. Agents' test suites written from specifications killed at most 55.5% of seeded faults, which is why a verifier must be tested with known-bad cases before it is trusted. Tension: this guide reports AI test-writing agents for fixes as helpful [BT]; the settings differ (tests for one fix, with a reproducing input, versus whole suites from a specification). |
| `why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai` | Mechanism behind this guide's weaknesses list. Training and evaluation reward guessing over abstaining, which helps explain confident incorrect results, permissive assumptions and invented package names. |
| `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code` | Agreement on responsibility and test-first. The Duck Book's golden rules (review LLM code yourself; you alone are responsible) match this guide's stance that humans are always responsible. Both put tests before logic. They differ on scope: the Duck Book requires review of all LLM-generated code, while this guide says vibe coding may be fine where code cannot have a security impact. |
| `uk-aqua-book-2025` | Agreement on independence and proportion. The Aqua Book's rule that assurer and analyst be independent matches this guide's independent verifier. Its proportionate assurance matches the guide's limit of human review to cases where failure can cause serious problems. |
| `microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook` | Agreement on review mechanics. Small focused pull requests, policies enforced in version control, and automation so humans review logic. These match this guide's *keep the change easy to review*, branch protection and hooks. |
| `he-cursor-velocity-complexity-2025` | Parallel finding at project scale. Persistent rises in warnings and complexity after agent adoption fit this guide's reported evidence that unreviewed AI iteration accumulates defects [BT]. |
| `becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025` | Parallel on misplaced confidence. Developers believed AI sped them up when it slowed them. This guide reports a study in which AI-assisted participants wrote less secure code yet believed it more secure [BT]. |
| `cucumber-bdd-gherkin` | Combine for Phase 1. Cucumber supplies examples as the executable specification of behaviour. This guide supplies the security half: a threat model that says what counts as a defect. |

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The guide is built largely from quotation. It cites about 140 outside works under its own bibliography keys: AI-lab and vendor reports, browser and OS-kernel project documentation, agency and industry guidance, practitioner posts, a private interview by the lead author, and many papers listed by arXiv link with no venue. None is held in this corpus, and none was read. Every finding marked `[BT]` here is the guide's report of that work, cited to the guide's section; the deep reference keeps the guide's keys for anyone tracing the chain. That covers the fix-success rates, the reviewer-consensus case study, the iteration-loop studies, the package-hallucination rates, the threat-model 90% figure, the untrusted-pull-request attacks and the pipeline designs. Where the guide quotes a corpus-held standard (OWASP ASVS, an OWASP agentic list), the integration table points to the corpus source independently and does not treat the guide's citation as that source.

**Named limits of the source.** (1) Its subject is unintentional vulnerabilities: finding, validating and fixing them with AI. It excludes building AI systems, AI-specific software risks, general secure coding and malicious software (Wheeler et al., § "Scope of this material"). Applying its finding-and-validation discipline to an agent's claims about feature work, tests or performance is this distillation's transfer, marked *by transfer* where it carries weight. (2) It dates its own evidence and expects specific models, services and statistics to change. The repository is actively edited; this distillation describes commit 82590814 only. (3) It records an open disagreement among its own sources on how prescriptive prompts should be, while all agree a threat model and tools are vital (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings"). (4) It reports criticism of its own headline fix-failure study alongside the study (Wheeler et al., § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities"). (5) Its CI-time target is hedged for operational technology and software that controls physical devices (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD"). (6) Several of its tools and two cited documents are OpenSSF's own or the lead author's; its "No endorsement intended" section applies.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** `[V]` quotations are copied from the deep reference's audited passages and match the converted source; the two blockquotes and the inline quotes were checked with `scripts/check-verbatim.py`. `[V] [BT]` marks words that are verbatim in the guide but are a third party's, as the guide quotes them. `[AP]` and `[AR]` mark the guide's own recommendations and arguments; the guide is a practitioner playbook, so its recommendations are assertions, not demonstrated results. Statistics keep their conditions where stated (complex vulnerabilities only; benchmark settings; model generations). Italic phrases in the What to Look For, Worked Example and Anti-patterns sections without quotation marks are this distillation's wording, not the source's. The deep reference's header records Pass I applied on 2026-10-15, but its closing "Audit status" line still says no Pass I has run; this distillation relies on the header and the hash stamp above.

## Runtime triggers this source addresses

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The story's acceptance criteria are prose ("works well", "handles errors") with no runnable check | For security properties: a clear definition is the precondition for telling defect from design, and the threat model should document what you do and don't care about [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing threat models") | Before the agent builds, write the properties this change must keep as statements a test can check. Without them, no reviewer can call anything a defect. |
| The agent is asked to "build X like Y" with no statement of what must not change | Separate preferences from invariants; invariants are enforced outside the AI (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | Name what must stay true, then decide where each rule is enforced. Anything only in the prompt is a preference. |
| Nobody can say who will use the change or what they will do with it | Agents do better when a project shares how the software is to be used, acceptable deployment scenarios and known problems [BT]; AIs tend to assume the most permissive deployment (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing threat models"; § "Reporting to externally maintained projects") | Write the deployment model down; otherwise the agent fills the gap with the loosest assumption. |
| The spec is long and the change is large | Narrow scope gives better results [BT]; keep changes easy to review; regressions track large rewrites [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes"; § "Approaching fixes") | Split it. Narrow tasks give better agent output and diffs a reviewer can follow. |
| The builder says "the agent will figure out the details" | AI tends to "run things out-of-order" [V] [BT] and guess the next step; it assumes the most permissive deployment (Wheeler et al., § "Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes"; § "Reporting to externally maintained projects") | The details it figures out are guesses you will not see. Give it the threat model and the context a new engineer would get. |

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The diff touches login, sessions, tokens or permissions | Prioritise code that enforces authentication or authorisation; examine invariants across re-authentication, token refresh and expiry, logout, revocation and role changes [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings") | Auth changes get the transition check: list what must hold before, during and after each state change, and test the paths that break it. |
| The change adds an LLM call, a prompt, a tool an agent can call, or memory | Injection is a named weakness; memory is "another input, not as authoritative truth" [V]; agentic systems are checked against an agentic top-ten list (Wheeler et al., § "Strengths and weaknesses"; § "Preparing AI"; § "Helping to identify findings") | Treat everything the new AI feature reads as data that can carry instructions. Then check the feature's shape against the agentic threat lists. |
| A migration, a delete or a bulk update is in the plan | High-impact actions (merging, deploying, modifying production, accessing sensitive resources) are explicit approval boundaries, enforced "in the tool or workflow rather than relying only on an instruction in the AI prompt" [V] [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Reporting to externally maintained projects") | This is an approval boundary. A human approves it, and the tool enforces that, not the prompt. |
| The change is business-critical, or complex enough that nobody can predict its effects | "Completely fixing complex vulnerabilities without creating new ones or breaking functionality is where today’s AI systems are weakest." [V] Human review is necessary where failures can cause serious problems (Wheeler et al., § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities"; § "Limit vibe coding") | Complex changes are where agents fail most. Plan expert human review before the build, not after. |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The agent proposes changing a test so the build goes green | Task verifiers are trusted computing base; agents must not be able to modify or bypass controls, since "the policy should live above the thing it governs." [V] [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | Block it. The checks that judge the agent's work sit above the agent; a human changes them, with a reason. |
| The tests were written by the same agent session after the code | Write a test that fails on the existing code first [BT]; validation is independent reproduction, not self-review [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"; § "Tips for validation") | Run those tests on the old code. If they pass there, they demonstrate nothing about this change. |
| A test checks the agent's output text rather than the system's state | "PoCs must measure target behaviour, not their own artifacts." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation") | A test that checks its own output proves the test ran. Assert on the system's state. |
| The suite passes, but nobody knows whether it would catch a wrong implementation | Test verifiers with known-good and known-bad cases; confirm checks fire on the broken version, not on benign input or the fixed version [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD"; § "Tips for validation") | Feed the suite a known-bad version. A verifier you have never seen fail is not yet evidence. |
| The suite takes minutes, so it runs rarely | Deterministic checks run on every change; "If CI takes too long, CI becomes the bottleneck." [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Turn findings into durable checks"; § "Preparing CI/CD") | Make the suite faster and run it on every change. A check that runs rarely protects rarely. |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| "Skip permissions, it's been fine for months" | "Do not depend on text commands alone to limit an AI." [V] Match isolation to capability; the guide reports models breaking out of test environments [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Need for sandboxes"; § "Implementing sandboxes") | Months of fine is a run of luck, not a control. Keep the sandbox at the strength of the most dangerous thing the agent can do. |
| The agent's environment can reach production credentials or data | Keep credential files out of reach; never give the AI a credential that would let it violate the gate; agents as distinct principals with only their role's permissions (Wheeler et al., § "Implementing sandboxes"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | Remove the reach, not just the intent. If the credential is not there, no prompt can misuse it. |
| The agent reads untrusted content (web pages, issues, emails) while holding tools | Repository and external text is data, not authority; separate analysis from action; no secrets or write tokens for agents on untrusted input [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Strengths and weaknesses"; § "Evaluate merge/pull requests") | Split the job: a low-privilege agent reads and reports; something trusted acts. |
| The agent adds a dependency nobody asked for | AI sometimes adds dependencies that don't exist or aren't the ones you think; confirm each is real, intended and needed (Wheeler et al., § "Have humans review the fix") | Check the package exists, is the one you meant, and is needed, before anything installs it. |
| The agent runs for an hour unattended and reports success | Record bounds "so that resource exhaustion or a timeout is not mistaken for successful completion" [V]; log AI activity where the AI cannot change it (Wheeler et al., § "Implementing sandboxes"; § "Preparing AI logging") | Read the log, not the summary. Did every step finish, and does the record show it? |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| "It worked first time", or a flaky check passed on retry | AI is non-deterministic, so don't depend on rerunning it; make deterministic checks (Wheeler et al., § "Run AI multiple times"; § "Turn findings into durable checks") | One success is one sample. What deterministic check now guards this? |
| A gate was skipped "just this once" | The gate must be "simple, certain, and clear to all participants" [V] and must not depend on the AI; where approval is required, enforce it in the tool (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch"; § "Reporting to externally maintained projects") | A gate that can be skipped by agreement is a preference. Record the skip on the pack, then make the gate enforced. |
| Lint and type errors are suppressed rather than fixed | "Use AI to prioritize such warnings, not to silently discard them." [V] Suppression comments are for confirmed false positives (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings"; § "Preparing CI/CD") | Every suppression is a finding until a human confirms it is a false positive. |
| The secrets scan or dependency audit is "noisy" so it was turned off | Minimise false positives, especially repeat ones; prioritise rather than discard; automate dependency updates (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD"; § "Helping to identify findings"; § "Preparing dependency updates") | Tune it, don't drop it: mark confirmed false positives and let the real ones through. |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The same session that wrote the code reviews it | The verifier should be independent of the discoverer, in a fresh container with no shared history [BT]; audit for agents able to approve each other's pull requests [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | A reviewer that shares the builder's context shares its mistakes. Start a fresh one with only the diff and the claims. |
| The reviewer's findings are long and nobody sorts them | Treat findings as possible problems; track them systematically; deduplicate by root cause; validate before acting (Wheeler et al., § "Managing findings"; § "Deduplicate"; § "Validate findings") | Each finding is a claim. Deduplicate, then confirm or refute each one before it blocks or passes the change. |
| The builder approves because reading the diff is too slow | Human review is necessary where failures can cause serious problems; reviewers focus on instance-only fixes, duplicated constructs and invented dependencies; humans should be "supported by automated processes" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Limit vibe coding"; § "Have humans review the fix"; § "Release and deploy") | Let AI review first and point you at the risky lines. Do not drop human review where failure would be serious. |
| The reviewer and builder agree too quickly | "Do not treat agreement among AI reviewers as proof." [V] Prompt the verifier to assume the claim is false (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation") | Quick agreement is the signal to ask for one executable demonstration. |
| The change "looks fine" but touches something with a history of incidents | Have the model cluster past bugs, check each past fix was complete, and look for similar problems (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings") | Ask what has broken here before, and check this change does not reopen it. |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The pack says "all tests pass" with no run record | Include provenance (revision, environment, invocation, assumptions) to "distinguish observed evidence from an AI-generated explanation" [V] [BT]; say what could not be built, tested or reproduced [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Helping to identify findings"; § "Reporting to externally maintained projects") | No run record, no claim. Return it for the record, and list what was not tested. |
| The client wants it today and the review is still open | The guide's answer to time pressure is faster gates, not skipped ones; it reports that a day-long regression suite forces skipping it to meet a tight deadline [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing CI/CD") | Say what is still open and what it risks. The fix for deadline pressure is a faster gate, which is work for next time, not a skip today. |
| Nobody could explain how this part works if the agent were unavailable | Humans are always responsible for what an AI does; a reported study argues that evaluating a complex patch often takes at least the understanding needed to write one [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Need for sandboxes"; § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities") | If no one can explain it, no one can evaluate it, and the signer is still responsible. |
| The builder signs because the last ten went fine | Don't expect the nth run to have zero new findings [BT]; the guide reports AI-assisted participants who wrote less secure code yet believed it more secure [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Run AI multiple times"; § "Limit vibe coding") | Past passes are not this change's evidence. What on this pack was demonstrated today? |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The release goes straight to everyone | Deploying and modifying production are approval boundaries enforced in the tool; keep a kill switch for the agents (Wheeler et al., § "Reporting to externally maintained projects"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | A human approves the deploy, the tool enforces it, and the agents can be stopped. How the rollout is staged is a harness rule, not this guide's. |
| Something went wrong after release | Write the failing test, fix the root cause, search for variants of the same pattern and class, update the threat model [BT], and turn the lesson into a durable check (Wheeler et al., § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"; § "Turn findings into durable checks") | Fix the class, not the instance, and leave behind a check that runs on every change. |

## Trigger extensions surfaced by this source

| Phase | Trigger | Content from this source | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | The agent's instructions file is the only thing enforcing a rule | Preferences in instructions, invariants outside; hooks enforce but do not replace a sandbox (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | Move the rule out of the prompt into a hook or permission the agent cannot edit. |
| 4 | The agent can read or delete its own logs | Log AI activity in a form the AI cannot delete or modify; logging cannot be changed for past events (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing AI logging") | Put logs where the agent cannot reach them, and set this up before you need it. |
| 4 | The agent cites its memory of the system for a security decision | Memory may be stale, wrong or shaped by untrusted input; prefer current code and reproducible evidence [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Preparing AI") | Check the claim against today's code, not the agent's memory of it. |
| 4 | The fixing agent was handed the reviewer's guess at a cause | Pass only what validation confirmed; reported incorrect guidance cut fix correctness by about 50 points [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Only provide correct information, especially if fully automated") | Give the fixer the failing test, not the theory. |
| 4 | The agent has rewritten the same area many times to satisfy a check | Limit iterations, prefer small changes, bring in a human; reported gains level off after about three rounds [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Approaching fixes") | Stop the loop at three and look at it yourself. |
| 5 | A gate reports nothing because it timed out, failed or was denied | Not evidence of no findings; record incomplete outcomes separately (Wheeler et al., § "Managing findings") | Incomplete is its own status. Rerun it; never file it as clean. |
| 3 | A check fires on the broken build but has not been run on the fixed build or on benign input | Confirm the check triggers on the specific failure, not on benign input, and not once fixed [BT] (Wheeler et al., § "Tips for validation") | Run the counterfactual before you trust the check. |
| 6 | Two agents with repository permissions can approve each other's changes | Reported case of agents undermining the human approval gate [BT]; audit workflows for indirect bypasses (Wheeler et al., § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") | Check who can approve what. An agent should never be the other agent's approver. |
| 6 | A review agent runs in CI on outside pull requests with secrets or write tokens | No secrets or write tokens, fewest tools, short-lived credentials, output untrusted, analysis separate from action (Wheeler et al., § "Evaluate merge/pull requests") | Strip the secrets and tools; the reviewer reads and reports, nothing more. |
| 6 | The fix adds a check at one call site, or blocks only the exact failing input | Root cause over instance; a separate agent tries variations of the failing input (Wheeler et al., § "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"; § "Have AI review the fix first") | Ask what the root cause is, and try variations before calling it fixed. |
| 6 | The agent wrote a new helper where the codebase already has one | AI often fails to reuse existing constructs, which "typically creates a maintenance nightmare" [V] (Wheeler et al., § "Have humans review the fix") | Point it at the existing helper. Duplicates are next year's drift. |
| 2 | The agent assigned the risk or severity rating | AI severity estimates run both too high and too low; a human reviews those that matter; answering specific questions with the threat model first helps (Wheeler et al., § "Triage") | Re-ask the rating through specific questions about reach, preconditions and blast radius, and have a human confirm it. |
